What an Average Can Hide

The mean is the sum divided by the count; the median is the middle position once the data are sorted. They answer different questions. To describe a dataset you should also look at its spread, its outliers, and the way the sample was drawn.
For the income data 1,2,3,4,90, the mean is 20 and the median is 3. Most entries lie far below the mean, which shows that a single measure of center is not enough to describe a distribution.
If 90 is changed to 900, what happens to the median and to the mean?
The median is still 3, while the mean becomes 182. The median is more robust to a single extreme value; that does not mean the mean should be abandoned in every setting.
Variance and Standard Deviation: The Scale of Variability

The variance is the average of the squared deviations of the data from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root, which carries the same units as the original data. Datasets with the same mean can have very different standard deviations; when the standard deviation is small, the data cluster near the mean. For a normal distribution, about 68% of the data fall within ±1 standard deviation of the mean; for unimodal, roughly symmetric data this is only a rough rule of thumb (normal distribution: see 09, Lesson 05).

For 1,2,3,4,90: the mean is 20, the squared deviations are 361+324+289+256+4900=6130, the variance is 1226, and the standard deviation is about 35. A single extreme value drives this measure of variability extremely high, in contrast with the robustness of the median.
Find the mean, variance, and standard deviation of 2,4,6,8.

The mean is 5; the deviations are −3,−1,1,3, the sum of squares is 20, the variance is 5, and the standard deviation is √5≈2.24. When the data are symmetric the deviations are symmetric too, and every point falls within ±2 standard deviations of the mean.
Correlation Alone Does Not Prove Causation

When two quantities move together, the explanation may be causation, a common cause, or a selection mechanism; for a modeling perspective on confounders, see the 16 Modeling branch. A randomized controlled trial uses random assignment to balance confounding factors as far as possible; its execution and its sample still have to be checked.

In summer, ice cream sales and the number of drownings may rise together. Hotter weather makes people buy ice cream and go swimming more often, so temperature is a common cause. Banning ice cream on the strength of the correlation alone does not imply that drownings would decrease.
Coffee drinkers score higher on exams — can we conclude directly that coffee raises scores?
No. Study time, sleep, and sample selection can all confound. First pin down the causal question, then consider a randomized experiment or a suitably designed observational study.
Point Estimation and Confidence Intervals

A statistic estimates a fixed unknown parameter; unbiasedness means its expectation equals that parameter. For independent identically distributed normal observations with known population standard deviation σ, X̄±1.96σ/√n has approximately 95% coverage. For nonnormal populations satisfying the central limit theorem conditions it is a large-sample approximation. Confidence describes coverage over repeated samples, not a 95% posterior probability for an already fixed μ.
With n=25, sample mean 10, and σ=5: the interval is 10±1.96×5/√25=10±1.96, that is, (8.04, 11.96).
What goes wrong if you plug in 1.96 directly when σ is unknown and the sample is small?

With unknown σ, estimate variance by s²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1). For independent identically distributed normal observations, (X̄−μ)/(s/√n) has a t distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom, giving X̄±t_{0.975,n−1}s/√n. Using 1.96 in a small normal sample usually undercovers. For a small nonnormal sample, replacing the quantile by t alone does not guarantee 95% coverage.
Hypothesis Testing

First state the null hypothesis H₀ (say, "no effect"), then compute, under H₀, the probability of a result at least this extreme (the p-value); if p is smaller than the significance level α fixed in advance, reject H₀. α is the Type I error rate; the probability of failing to reject when rejection is called for is the Type II error rate β, and the power of the test, 1−β, depends on the sample size and the true effect size. The p-value is not "the probability that H₀ is true", and it does not measure the size of an effect.

A fair coin lands heads 18 times in 20 tosses: under H₀: p=0.5, P(≥18)=(C(20,18)+C(20,19)+C(20,20))/2²⁰=(190+20+1)/1048576≈0.0002, so "fair" is rejected (here as a one-sided test for a bias toward heads; the two-sided p-value is doubled, and the conclusion is unchanged).
Is p=0.03 the same thing as "the null hypothesis has only a 3% chance of being true"?

No. The p-value is "the probability of data this extreme if H₀ is true" — the conditioning points the other way; P(H₀|data) also depends on the prior and on the power of the test. A small p-value says that the data conflict with H₀; it does not directly give the probability of H₀.
Least Squares Regression

Fit the line y=a+bx to the scatter of points (xᵢ,yᵢ), choosing a and b to minimize the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ−a−bxᵢ)². The two normal equations give a closed form: b=Cov(x,y)/Var(x) (covariance: see 09, Lesson 06) and a=ȳ−bx̄. R² is the proportion of the variance explained by the regression. The geometric interpretation of least squares is "projection onto the column space": see 04, Lesson 08. The slope formula requires Var(x)>0. With an intercept and nonconstant responses, R²=1−residual sum of squares/total sum of squares. This interpretation cannot be transferred indiscriminately to models without an intercept.
Points (1,2),(2,3),(3,5): x̄=2, ȳ=10/3, Cov=1, Var(x)=2/3, giving b=1.5 and a=1/3, so the line is y=1/3+1.5x.
Why minimize the "squares" instead of the absolute values?

Squared loss is smooth, and this linear model has a unique closed-form fit when the design matrix has full column rank. It also corresponds to maximum likelihood under independent homoscedastic Gaussian errors. Absolute loss is nondifferentiable at zero residual and usually more robust to extremes; general linear regression requires different optimization methods. It is false that absolute loss never has a closed-form solution: for a constant-only fit, any median minimizes it.
Introduction to Bayesian Statistics

Frequentists treat the parameter as a fixed but unknown quantity and reason through sampling distributions; Bayesians treat the parameter as a random variable: assign a prior distribution and update it with the data to obtain the posterior — posterior∝likelihood×prior. Bayes' rule in 09 is the single-event version; here the update operates on a whole distribution over the parameter θ. The prior is a subjective input written out in the open; it can be examined and subjected to sensitivity analysis — which is why it is both criticized and prized.

For the heads probability θ of a coin: take the prior Beta(2,2) (centered, with a slight preference for fairness). After observing 8 heads and 2 tails, the posterior is Beta(10,4) with mean 10/14≈0.71 — ten observations pull the prior markedly toward the data.
With prior Beta(1,1) (the uniform distribution) and 3 heads against 1 tail observed, what is the posterior mean? And what if a further 20 tosses give 15 heads and 5 tails?

From Beta(1,1), observing 3 heads and 1 tail gives Beta(4,2), mean 4/6=2/3. Adding 15 heads and 5 tails yields Beta(19,7), mean 19/26≈0.73. In this conjugate model, the relative weight of a fixed prior's pseudocounts decreases with sample size. General asymptotic agreement with frequentist methods needs model, identifiability and prior-support conditions; it is not guaranteed for arbitrary priors or models.

From Laws of Change to Exponential Growth

y′=ky says that the rate of change is proportional to the current amount. Given the initial value y(0)=y₀, the solution is y=y₀eᵏᵗ. The equation describes the law; the initial value selects the particular trajectory.

Take k=0.1 and y₀=100; then y(t)=100e⁰·¹ᵗ. To verify, differentiate to get 10e⁰·¹ᵗ, which is exactly 0.1y (the differentiation rule for the exponential function: see 06, Lesson 03), and check that the value at t=0 is 100.
What is the solution of y′=−2y, y(0)=3? What happens to it in the long run?
y=3e⁻²ᵗ. As t tends to positive infinity it tends to 0, yet at every finite time it is still positive. The model may be a poor fit for a small number of discrete individuals.
Separable Equations: Pulling the Rate of Change Apart

When y′=g(x)h(y), write y′ as dy/dx and "separate": dy/h(y)=g(x)dx, then integrate both sides to solve (the step is justified by integration by substitution, see 06, Lesson 05). Exponential growth, the logistic equation, Newton's law of cooling, and radioactive decay are all instances — this is the first method that generalizes exponential growth. Before dividing by h(y), find equilibrium solutions with h(y)=0 so none are lost. Logarithmic antiderivatives generally use ln|·|, with signs determined on the solution interval.
y′=y(1−y), y(0)=1/2: since 1/[y(1−y)]=1/y+1/(1−y), integrating gives ln[y/(1−y)]=x+C, and solving for y yields y=1/(1+Ae⁻ˣ); the initial value gives A=1, so the S-shaped curve is y=1/(1+e⁻ˣ).
Solve Newton's law of cooling T′=−k(T−T₀); according to what law does the temperature difference evolve? (Used directly in the physics lessons of 15 Mathematical Physics.)

Assume k>0 and constant ambient temperature T₀. If T(0)≠T₀, separation gives ln|T−T₀|=−kt+C and hence T=T₀+(T(0)−T₀)e^(−kt), valid both above and below ambient temperature. If T(0)=T₀, the equilibrium T≡T₀ must be retained separately rather than lost when dividing by T−T₀. The absolute temperature difference decays exponentially.
Direction Fields and Initial Value Problems

A first-order equation y′=f(t,y) assigns a slope to each point (t,y); drawing these little line segments produces the direction field, and a solution curve is a curve that fits the direction field everywhere. The initial value y(t₀)=y₀ sets the starting point. When f and ∂f/∂y (differentiate with respect to y, treating t as a constant; partial derivatives: see 06, Lesson 09) are continuous, the solution exists and is unique locally — exactly one solution curve passes through each point.

y′=−2y: the higher up, the more steeply the segments point downward, and in the solution family y=Ce⁻²ᵗ the curves for different C never intersect. If two solution curves both passed through the same point, they would be two solutions of the same initial value problem, contradicting existence and uniqueness, so they must be the same curve — the fact that "each point has only one slope" is not by itself enough to rule out two curves meeting tangentially. Advancing step by step along the direction field is Euler's method: see 12, Lesson 03.
Why can a solution of y′=y² run away in finite time? Does this contradict existence and uniqueness?

The solution starting from y(0)=1 is y=1/(1−t), which tends to infinity at t=1 (blow-up in finite time). Existence and uniqueness is a local guarantee: a solution can escape the region under discussion in finite time, so it has to be examined interval by interval.
Equilibrium Is Not the Same as Stability
For an autonomous equation y′=f(y), an equilibrium satisfies f(y*)=0. Stability asks what happens after a small deviation, not merely whether the system can sit still there.

The equilibria of y′=y(1−y) are 0 and 1. The arrows point up for 0<y<1 and down for y>1, so trajectories near the positive half-axis approach 1, while a small positive perturbation of 0 moves away from 0.
For y′=−y, is 0 an attracting or a repelling equilibrium? Explain in terms of the solution.
Attracting. y(t)=y(0)e⁻ᵗ approaches 0 from both the positive and the negative side. The verdict is taken with respect to evolution in forward time.
First-Order Linear Equations and Integrating Factors

Multiply the standard form y′+p(t)y=q(t) on both sides by μ(t)=e^(∫p dt) and the left-hand side becomes exactly (μy)′, so a single integration solves the equation. This is the technique of "completing an incomplete derivative"; the choice of μ is dictated entirely by p.
y′+2y=e^(−t): μ=e^(2t), so (e^(2t)y)′=e^t; integrating gives e^(2t)y=e^t+C, hence y=e^(−t)+Ce^(−2t).
Solve y′+y=t with initial value y(0)=1.
μ=e^t, so (e^t y)′=te^t; integration by parts (see 06, Lesson 05) gives e^t y=(t−1)e^t+C, hence y=t−1+Ce^(−t). Substituting y(0)=1 gives C=2. Check: y′+y=(1−2e^(−t))+(t−1+2e^(−t))=t ✓.
Second-Order Equations with Constant Coefficients

Trying y=e^(rt) in y″+by′+cy=0 leads to the characteristic equation r²+br+c=0. Two distinct real roots give a combination of exponentials; a repeated root gives (c₁+c₂t)e^(rt) (the extra factor of t is what yields two independent solutions); complex roots α±βi give e^(αt)(c₁cosβt+c₂sinβt) (by Euler's formula e^(iθ)=cosθ+i·sinθ, which follows from the series expansions in the 06 lesson on series; for the geometry of eigenvalues, see 04, Lesson 07). The three damping regimes of the spring equation correspond exactly to the three kinds of roots.
y″−y=0: r=±1, so y=c₁e^t+c₂e^(−t). y″+4y=0: r=±2i, so y=c₁cos2t+c₂sin2t, in agreement with the lesson on simple harmonic oscillation.
What is the general solution of y″+2y′+y=0? What damping regime is this?

r²+2r+1=(r+1)² is a repeated root, so y=(c₁+c₂t)e^(−t). This is critical damping: with slightly less damping the roots become complex and the solution starts to oscillate; with more, it decays slowly as a pure exponential. The repeated root is exactly the boundary between the two regimes.
The Phase Plane and Linear Systems

Two coupled first-order equations, x′=ax+by and y′=cx+dy, combine into v′=Av; plotting (x,y) at each instant in the phase plane gives the trajectories. The origin is an equilibrium, and its type is decided by the eigenvalues: two negative real numbers = a stable node; one positive and one negative = a saddle point; complex numbers with negative real part = a stable spiral; purely imaginary numbers = a center (closed orbits). This is the gateway where "dynamical systems" begins to live up to its name, and the linear algebra promised in the prerequisites is cashed in here.

Simple harmonic oscillation x″=−4x turns into x′=v, v′=−4x, i.e. A=[[0,1],[−4,0]], whose characteristic equation λ²+4=0 gives λ=±2i: a center whose trajectories are concentric ellipses — the geometric image of conservation of energy (the lesson on simple harmonic oscillation in 15 Mathematical Physics).
What shape are the trajectories of A=diag(1,−1) (that is, x′=x, y′=−y)? What type is the origin?

The solutions are x=c₁eᵗ and y=c₂e^(−t), so the product xy=c₁c₂ is constant: a family of hyperbolas, and the origin is a saddle point. Trajectories flee along one eigen-direction and approach along the other — the signs of the eigenvalues let you read off the entire qualitative story.
Bifurcations: How a Parameter Changes the Phase Portrait

In a system with a parameter, x′=f(x;r), an event where the qualitative structure (the number of equilibria and their stability) changes abruptly as r varies is called a bifurcation. The simplest saddle-node bifurcation is x′=r−x²: for r<0 there is no equilibrium and trajectories slide all the way down; at r=0 a semi-stable equilibrium appears at 0; for r>0 it splits into two equilibria, one stable (√r) and one unstable (−√r). A bifurcation diagram plots the equilibria as curves against r: a solid curve for the stable branch, a dashed curve for the unstable branch.

r=1: the equilibria are −1 (f′=−2x=2>0, unstable) and 1 (f′=−2, stable). As the parameter sweeps from positive to negative, the two equilibria collide head-on at r=0 and annihilate each other — at the critical value the system has "nowhere to stop".
For x′=rx−x² (the logistic equation with a parameter), how does the structure of equilibria change as r goes from negative to positive?

The equilibria are 0 and r. For r<0: 0 is stable (f′(0)=r<0), while r is negative and unstable; for r>0: 0 loses stability (f′(0)=r>0), while r turns positive and stable — a transcritical bifurcation: the two equilibria exchange stability at r=0, and as the parameter crosses the critical value the system (on the half-line x≥0) switches from "collapsing to zero" to "sustaining itself". This is where the logistic equation of Lesson 04 meets the logistic model of 16 Modeling.
Difference Equations and the Logistic Map

A discrete-time system xₙ₊₁=f(xₙ) evolves by iteration. A fixed point satisfies x*=f(x*), and |f′(x*)|<1 is sufficient for local attraction. The logistic map xₙ₊₁=rxₙ(1−xₙ) is usually studied for 0≤r≤4 and 0≤x₀≤1. For interior initial values, 0<r≤1 leads to 0, and 1<r<3 to (r−1)/r; endpoints 0 and 1 need separate treatment. Period-doubling begins at r=3, with an accumulation point near 3.56995. Beyond it, chaotic regimes coexist with periodic windows; not every r>3.57 is chaotic.
r=2, x₀=0.3: 0.3→0.42→0.4872→0.4997→… converging to 0.5=(r−1)/r; at that point f′=2(1−2×0.5)=0, so it is superstable. With the same r and x₀=0.9: 0.9→0.18→0.2952→0.4161→… still converges to 0.5.
For r=3.2, is the fixed point (r−1)/r=0.6875 stable? What is the long-run behavior likely to be?

|f′|=|3.2×(1−2×0.6875)|=1.2>1, so the fixed point loses stability; the orbit approaches a cycle of period 2 (bouncing back and forth between two values). That period-2 cycle destabilizes into period 4 at r≈3.45, then 8, 16, … — period-doubling on the road to chaos. Even a deterministic system can "look random".
Ergodicity: Time Averages Equal Space Averages

A system is ergodic if the long-time average along almost every orbit equals the average taken with respect to the invariant distribution: lim(1/T)∫₀ᵀ g(x(t))dt=∫g dμ. The physical picture: the long-run experience of one molecule in a cup of coffee ≈ a statistical snapshot of all the molecules — follow one orbit long enough, and there is no need to sweep the whole space. Ergodicity is weaker than mixing: ergodicity guarantees only that the averages agree, while mixing further demands that the system gradually forget its initial value.

Consider x↦x+α (mod 1) with uniform measure on the circle. If α is irrational, every starting point has an equidistributed orbit, and time averages of continuous observables equal circle averages. If α=p/q is rational, all orbits are periodic and the rotation is not ergodic for uniform measure. A finite irreducible Markov chain also has ergodic time averages, while convergence of its step-by-step distribution additionally needs aperiodicity. These two kinds of convergence are different.
For an irrational rotation, why does the time average along a single orbit equal the average over the circle? What are the exceptions in "almost every orbit"?

For irrational α and continuous observables, Weyl equidistribution gives equality of time and uniform space averages for every starting point, including rational ones. There are no periodic orbits from rational starts: returning after q steps would require qα to be an integer. The general ergodic theorem for integrable observables guarantees almost-everywhere convergence and permits a null exceptional set; that weaker guarantee should not be mistaken for an actual exception in this stronger example.

Floating Point: Why 0.1+0.2 ≠ 0.3

Floating-point numbers usually use a finite binary significand and an exponent. Since 0.1 has no finite binary representation, common IEEE 754 operations round to representable numbers rather than simply truncating. Subtracting nearby approximate values can amplify relative error already present in the inputs; not every subtraction itself incurs a large new rounding error. Compare approximate results with suitable absolute and relative tolerances, for example |a−b|≤atol+rtol·max(|a|,|b|), chosen for the problem scale.

1−0.9999999: the true value is 10⁻⁷, but 0.9999999 itself already carries a representation error on the order of 10⁻¹⁶, and after the subtraction the relative error is amplified enormously. Comparing floating-point numbers should be written |a−b|<tolerance, not a==b.
Summing 1/n for n=1 to 10000 — is it usually more accurate to add from small to large, or from large to small? Why?

Small-to-large refers to term values: add 1/10000,1/9999,…,1, rather than increasing the index from 1 to 10000. For these positive terms, combining small values first usually reduces loss when tiny terms are added to a large partial sum. This is not a universal optimality guarantee for signed sequences. Pairwise or compensated summation can also reduce error; operation order is part of a floating-point algorithm.
Why Bisection Is Reliable

A continuous function taking opposite signs at the two ends of an interval has at least one zero there. Bisection keeps the half that still contains the sign change. It promises nothing about uniqueness of the zero, but every step halves the length of the bracketing interval.
For f(x)=x²−2, start from [1,2]. The midpoint 1.5 gives 0.25>0, so keep [1,1.5]; then 1.25 gives a negative value, so keep [1.25,1.5].
Starting from an interval of length 1, how long is the interval after 10 bisections? What is the bound on the midpoint error?
The interval has length 1/1024, and the midpoint is at most 1/2048 away from any root inside it. Continuity must hold, and the retained interval must contain a root.
Euler's Method Is a Local Straight-Line Prediction
To solve y′=f(t,y), step forward via yₙ₊₁=yₙ+h f(tₙ,yₙ). This is a tangent-line prediction; both the step size and stability affect the result.
For y′=y, y(0)=1 with step size 0.5, two steps give 1.5 and 2.25; the exact value is y(1)=e≈2.718. Local estimates accumulate error.
For y′=−2y with h=1 and h=0.25, what are the one-step factors? What does this show?
The factors are −1 and 0.5. The former produces non-decaying oscillation, the latter decays. The exact solution always decays exponentially, so too large a step can change the qualitative behavior.
Newton's Method

To solve f(x)=0: at xₙ approximate f by its tangent; the tangent's zero becomes the next iterate: xₙ₊₁=xₙ−f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ). Near a simple root it converges quadratically (the number of correct digits roughly doubles per step), but it depends on a good initial guess, and it fails where the derivative is near zero or the iterates oscillate back and forth.

To compute √2, solve x²−2=0 with xₙ₊₁=(xₙ+2/xₙ)/2. Starting from x₀=1 gives x₁=1.5, x₂≈1.416667, x₃≈1.414215686. After the third update the absolute error is about 2.1×10⁻⁶, illustrating rapid error reduction near a simple root. Speed comparisons need a stated initial guess, interval and error criterion.
What happens when iterating f(x)=x³−2x+2 from x₀=0? What does this show?

With f′=3x²−2: x₁=0−2/(−2)=1, then x₂=1−1/1=0 — the iteration cycles between 0 and 1 forever. Newton's method comes with only a local convergence guarantee; globally it can oscillate without advancing. In practice, screen the initial guess, or mix with bisection as a safety net.
Numerical Integration: Trapezoidal and Simpson's Rules

The trapezoidal rule treats f as a straight line: ∫≈(b−a)(f(a)+f(b))/2, with composite error O(h²). Simpson's rule fits a parabola through three points: (b−a)/6·[f(a)+4f(midpoint)+f(b)], with composite error O(h⁴) — at the same number of nodes, the accuracy jumps by an order of magnitude. These composite error orders require suitably bounded second and fourth derivatives, respectively, on a fixed integration interval. Composite Simpson quadrature normally also requires an even number of equal subintervals.
∫₀¹1/(1+x)dx=ln2≈0.6931. Trapezoidal: (1+0.5)/2=0.75, an error of about 8%. Simpson: (1/6)(1+4×(2/3)+0.5)≈0.6944, an error of 0.2%.
Is the trapezoidal rule exact for linear functions? Is Simpson's rule exact for cubics?

The trapezoid rule is exact for polynomials of degree at most 1, so its algebraic degree of precision is 1. Simpson's rule is exact through degree 3 and has degree of precision 3; its panel error involves a fourth derivative. Algebraic precision differs from composite convergence order: the respective errors are O(h²) and O(h⁴), under suitable smoothness assumptions.
Interpolation: The Lagrange Polynomial

Through n+1 points with distinct x-coordinates there passes exactly one polynomial of degree at most n. The Lagrange form: the basis function Lᵢ equals 1 at the i-th point and 0 at all the others, and p=ΣyᵢLᵢ. Interpolation is not approximation: high-degree interpolation on equally spaced nodes oscillates near the ends (the Runge phenomenon), so splines switch to low-degree pieces, trading 'lower degree' for stability.

The quadratic through (0,1), (1,3), (2,2) is p(x)=−1.5x²+3.5x+1: check p(0)=1, p(1)=3, p(2)=2. It is assembled from basis functions such as L₀=(x−1)(x−2)/2 — each basis function 'claims' one point and vanishes at the others.
What does linear interpolation through (1,2) and (3,5) give at x=2? Is it the average of the two endpoint values?

p(2)=2+(5−2)/(3−1)×(2−1)=3.5 — exactly the average of the endpoints (a coincidence of the equally spaced midpoint). With three or more points, the interpolant is determined by all the nodes; it is not a pointwise average. Interpolation answers 'passing through', while regression (Lesson 06 of 10) answers 'passing nearest': use interpolation for exact data, regression for noisy data.
Numerical Linear Algebra: Condition Numbers and Stability

Errors in solving Ax=b come from more than rounding: the relative error of the input b can be amplified by as much as the condition number κ(A)=‖A‖·‖A⁻¹‖. A large κ is called ill-conditioned — the problem itself is hard, independent of the algorithm; the algorithm's stability is responsible for 'not ruining a good problem'. Practical points: use pivoting in elimination, and iterative methods (such as conjugate gradient) for large sparse matrices. Standard conjugate gradients require a real symmetric positive-definite matrix; sparsity alone is insufficient.

A=[[1,1],[1,1.0001]], κ≈4×10⁴. The true solution for b=(2,2) is (2,0); perturbing b to (2,2.0001) changes the solution to (1,1) — a perturbation of b on the order of five parts in a hundred thousand completely changes the solution.
Using the example above, estimate ‖Δb‖/‖b‖ and ‖Δx‖/‖x‖. By roughly what factor was the error amplified? Is it the same order of magnitude as κ?

Use the Euclidean 2-norm throughout: ‖Δb‖₂/‖b‖₂=0.0001/√8≈3.54×10⁻⁵ and ‖Δx‖₂/‖x‖₂=√2/2≈0.707. The amplification is about 2×10⁴, comparable to and below κ₂(A)≈4×10⁴. Do not mix norms between numerators, denominators or the two sides when checking the bound. A small residual need not imply a small solution error in an ill-conditioned problem.

The Optimum Depends on the Feasible Region

An optimization problem consists of variables, an objective function, and constraints. However attractive the objective, a point that violates a constraint is not a candidate solution. A local optimum compares only against nearby points; a global optimum compares against every feasible point.
Minimize (x−3)² over 0≤x≤5: the optimum is 3. Change the constraint to 0≤x≤2 and the optimum moves to 2. The unconstrained stationary point need not be feasible.
Minimize (x−2)² over 0≤x≤1. What is the answer?
x=1, with objective value 1: within the interval, the closer x is to 2, the smaller the squared distance. Mechanically setting the derivative to zero would yield the infeasible point 2.
Why Gradient Descent Can Overshoot

For a differentiable function, the gradient gives the direction of steepest local ascent; this lesson stays one-dimensional (the multivariable gradient appears in Lesson 09 of 06, and convergence in several dimensions is governed by the eigenvalues of the second-derivative matrix — see Lesson 07 of 04). The descent iteration reads x_new=x−ηf′(x), with a positive step size η. It is not magic that guarantees a global optimum for every function.
For f(x)=x² the iteration becomes x_new=(1−2η)x. If 0<η<1, the absolute factor is below 1, so the iterates tend to 0; at η=1 they merely bounce back and forth; for η>1 they typically diverge.
With η=0.25 and x₀=4, what are the first two iterates?
The factor is 1/2, so x₁=2 and x₂=1. The function value drops from 16 to 4 and then to 1. The convergence condition comes from this specific quadratic.
Convex Sets and Convex Functions

A convex set contains the line segment between any two of its points. A function on a convex domain is convex if f(λx+(1−λ)y)≤λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y) for 0≤λ≤1. A convex objective over a convex feasible set makes every local minimum global. Convexity is an important sufficient structure, not the only possible class with that property.

Both x² and eˣ are convex. For x³ the second derivative is 6x, so it is concave on the negative half-line and convex on the positive half-line, with an inflection at 0; it is not globally convex. Check derivative signs rather than relying only on a sketch.
Prove that a local minimum of a convex function must be a global minimum.

Suppose x* is a local minimum yet some y has f(y)<f(x*). Choose a small λ so that z=λy+(1−λ)x* lies in the neighborhood of x*; convexity gives f(z)≤λf(y)+(1−λ)f(x*)<f(x*), contradicting local minimality. Convexity pulls 'better far away' into 'better nearby'.
Linear Programming and Vertices

When the objective and all constraints are linear, the problem is a linear program, in standard form: optimize cᵀx subject to Ax≤b, x≥0; the feasible region is a convex polyhedron. Basic fact: a bounded optimum is attained at a vertex — so 'searching over a continuum' reduces to 'comparing finitely many vertices', which is where the simplex method comes from.
max x+y subject to x+2y≤4, x≥0, y≥0: the feasible region is a triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (0,2) and objective values 0, 4, 2 — the optimum sits at (4,0).
Add the constraint x≤3 to the previous problem. How do the optimum and its value change?

The feasible region becomes the quadrilateral (0,0), (3,0), (3,0.5), (0,2) with objective values 0, 3, 3.5, 2; the optimum moves to the new vertex (3,0.5). The optimum is still attained at a vertex — slice off one corner, and the optimum simply relocates to the new corner.
Duality and KKT: Viewing the Optimum from the Other Side

The dual of min cᵀx subject to Ax≥b,x≥0 is max bᵀy subject to Aᵀy≤c,y≥0. Weak duality bounds feasible objective values; when the primal is feasible with a finite optimum, strong duality makes the optimal values equal. Optimal multipliers describe local sensitivity; signs depend on constraint conventions and changes of optimal basis matter. Nonlinear KKT conditions comprise primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity and complementary slackness. Necessity requires a constraint qualification. For differentiable convex problems, satisfying KKT is sufficient for global optimality; with Slater's condition, KKT characterizes optimality.
The dual of max x+y s.t. x+2y≤4, x,y≥0 (Lesson 04) is min 4w s.t. w≥1, 2w≥1, w≥0, with optimum w=1 and value 4 — equal to the primal optimum 4. The same mountain, climbed from two sides.
In the example above, loosen the right-hand side 4 to 4.5. Roughly how much does the optimal value change? Does it agree with the shadow price w=1?

The optimal vertex moves from (4,0) to (4.5,0) and the value from 4 to 4.5 — an increment of 0.5=1×0.5, exactly w×Δb. Within the range where the constraint remains active, the shadow price forecasts the sensitivity exactly; reading the dual variable is reading 'what the constraint is worth'.
Game Theory: Nash Equilibrium

A game = players, strategy sets, and payoff functions. A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile with 'no profitable unilateral deviation': each player's choice is a best response to the others' strategies. A pure-strategy equilibrium may fail to exist (rock–paper–scissors), but Nash's theorem guarantees that every finite game has a mixed-strategy equilibrium. Equilibrium does not mean collective optimality: in the prisoner's dilemma the equilibrium is mutual defection, worse than mutual cooperation — the crack between individual and collective rationality.

Prisoner's dilemma: both stay silent → 1 year each; one defects → the defector walks free and the other serves 10 years; both defect → 5 years each. Whatever the other does, defecting is lighter (0<1 and 5<10), so (defect, defect) is the unique equilibrium — 5 years each, worse than the 1 year each under mutual silence.

Matching pennies: each player chooses heads or tails. If they match, A gets 1 and B gets −1; otherwise A gets −1 and B gets 1. Find the mixed-strategy equilibrium and expected payoffs. Does this game have the same number of strategies as rock-paper-scissors?

Independent fair randomization is an equilibrium: against a uniform opponent, either pure action has expected payoff 0, so no unilateral change improves it. A bias could be exploited by the opponent. Equilibrium expected payoffs are therefore 0. Matching pennies has two strategies per player and rock-paper-scissors has three, so the games are not isomorphic. Both illustrate mixed strategies, but symmetry alone does not make every game's payoff zero.

Algorithmic Complexity Is About Growth

Complexity describes how resource use grows as the input size grows. O(n) is an asymptotic upper bound, not an exact number of seconds; when analyzing an algorithm, say whether the worst case, the average case, or some other scenario is meant.

Binary search on a sorted array halves the pool of candidates at each step. For n=1024, about 10 halvings leave a single item, exhibiting logarithmic growth; searching an unsorted array item by item must, in the worst case, examine all n items.
When the input size doubles, by roughly what factor does the dominant work of a linear algorithm and of a quadratic algorithm grow?
About 2× and 4×, respectively, provided one compares dominant terms at sufficiently large sizes. Actual running times are also affected by constants, hardware, and the input.
Information Content and Surprise

The self-information of an event of probability p is −log₂p, measured in bits. A rare event, when it occurs, delivers more information; entropy is the probability-weighted average of self-information.

Each outcome of a fair coin carries 1 bit of information, so the entropy is 1. A certain outcome has probability 1 and self-information 0. A binary random variable has maximum entropy at p=1/2; the more it favors one outcome, the more predictable it is.
Among four equally likely outcomes, how many bits of information does observing one outcome carry?
−log₂(1/4)=2 bits. This corresponds to the two ideal binary choices needed to distinguish four outcomes.
Automata and Formal Languages

A finite automaton has finitely many states, updates its state for each input symbol, and accepts according to its final state. It recognizes precisely the regular languages. It can track finite-state information such as parity, but cannot recognize {aⁿbⁿ:n≥1}, which requires distinguishing unboundedly many prefix lengths. It is too broad to say automata cannot count at all.

Recognizing "binary strings containing an even number of 1s": two states, even/odd; reading a 1 switches between them, reading a 0 stays put, and the accepting state is even. On input 1011 the machine passes even→odd→odd→even→odd and ends in the odd state, so it rejects (three 1s).
Why can a finite automaton not recognize {aⁿbⁿ : n≥1}?

Matching the b's requires remembering how many a's were seen; finitely many states can distinguish only finitely many prefixes, so as n grows without bound two different prefixes must fall into the same state, after which the machine gives the same verdict when either is followed by the same string of b's — yet aⁿbⁿ demands exactly that distinction. What is missing is the capacity for unbounded counting.
Computability and P/NP

Computable means that an algorithm exists which always halts and returns an answer; by the diagonal argument, the halting problem is not computable. P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time, and NP is the class for which a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time; P⊆NP is clear, but whether the two are equal is an open Millennium Problem. NP-complete problems (such as SAT) are the hardest members of NP: every NP problem can be reduced to them in polynomial time.

Complexity concerns families with growing input size. Generalized Sudoku, whose board size can grow, has an NP-complete solvability decision problem. Fixed 9×9 Sudoku has only finitely many inputs, so it is not by itself an asymptotic hardness example. A proposed generalized solution is polynomially checkable; a general polynomial-time solving algorithm relates to P versus NP. SAT is NP-complete by the Cook–Levin theorem.
Why does "fast to verify" not imply "fast to solve"?

Verification checks one proposed candidate; solving must find a suitable one. A large candidate space alone is not a lower-bound proof, because an algorithm might exploit structure rather than enumerate it. For NP-complete problems no general polynomial-time algorithm or proof of its impossibility is known; P≠NP remains unproved. Cryptographic security typically requires specific average-case hardness assumptions, not merely P≠NP.
RSA: How Number Theory Encrypts

Classroom RSA uses distinct primes p,q, n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1). Choose e coprime to φ(n) and use extended Euclid to find ed≡1 (mod φ(n)). A message representative satisfies 0≤m<n; encryption is c=mᵉ mod n and decryption is cᵈ mod n. Euler's theorem proves correctness for m coprime to n; for arbitrary m, prove it modulo p and q and combine by the Chinese remainder theorem. Factoring is one known attack route; RSA inversion has not been proved equivalent to factoring. This is deterministic raw RSA arithmetic; actual encryption schemes need specified encodings such as RSAES-OAEP.
A toy version: p=3, q=11, n=33, φ=20; take e=7 and d=3 (21≡1 (mod 20)). For the message m=5: 5²=25, 5⁴≡31, 5⁷≡5⁴·5²·5≡31×25×5≡14 (mod 33); decryption gives 14³=2744≡5 (mod 33).
Why does "factoring n" amount to "breaking RSA"? Which steps lead from n=pq to recovering d?

Factoring n yields p,q and hence φ(n); invert the public e modulo φ(n) to recover a private exponent d. Thus factoring is sufficient to recover a private key, not a proof that every attack must first factor n. Raw RSA's determinism, encoding errors and implementation flaws can also expose messages. The toy example connects primes, modular inverses, Euler and CRT; it is not a deployable encryption scheme.
Error-Correcting Codes: From Repetition to Hamming

An error-correcting code uses a subset of legal words and decodes by distance. The repetition code {000,111} corrects at most one flipped bit at rate 1/3. In the even-parity Hamming (7,4) code, parity positions 1,2,4 check {1,3,5,7}, {2,3,6,7}, {4,5,6,7}. If their violation flags are (s₁,s₂,s₄), the error position is s₁+2s₂+4s₄, or binary (s₄s₂s₁)₂. This guarantee assumes at most one bit error; a zero syndrome does not rule out multiple errors.

If (s₁,s₂,s₄)=(1,0,1), the error position is 1+0+4=5. To check bit order, use (1,1,0): the position is 1+2=3, binary 011, not 110 read as 6. Under a single-bit error, flipping that position restores the word. The information rate is 4/7.
The repetition code receives 010: which codeword is decided on? Why is it powerless against two bits flipping at once?

It is at distance 1 from 000 and distance 2 from 111, so decode to 000. If two bits are wrong (say 011), it is closer to 111 instead and the decision flips — error-correcting power is governed by the minimum distance between codewords: distance 3 corrects 1 error, and correcting t errors requires distance 2t+1. Coding theory is where information theory (Lesson 02) converges with linear algebra.

Dimensional Analysis: First Check Whether a Formula Is Possible

The two sides of a physical equation must agree in dimension. Dimensional correctness does not guarantee that a formula is right, but a dimensional error suffices to veto it. Length L, time T, and mass M can be combined.

Velocity has dimension L/T and acceleration L/T². The candidate formula gt for free-fall displacement has dimension L/T, not a length; gt² has dimension L and at least passes the dimensional check, with the coefficient still to be fixed by dynamics.
Could the period of a spring be proportional to √(m/k)? Given F=kx.
The dimension of k is (M L/T²)/L=M/T², so √(m/k) has dimension T. It passes the check; the full period 2π√(m/k) requires solving the equation.
Newton's Second Law and Simple Harmonic Oscillation

Newton's second law F=ma is the second-order equation m x″=F — precisely the standard object of the "second-order equations with constant coefficients" in 11 (characteristic roots ±iω). A linear spring F=−kx gives x″=−(k/m)x, with general solution x(t)=A cos(ωt)+B sin(ωt), ω=√(k/m). The amplitude is set by the initial conditions, while the period 2π√(m/k) is independent of the amplitude (isochronism).
With m=1, k=4, x(0)=1, x′(0)=0: x=cos 2t, with period 2π/2=π. Verify that x″=−4cos 2t=−4x. Doubling the initial values gives 2cos 2t, still oscillating with the same period.
If k and m are both multiplied by 4, how does the period change? And if only m is multiplied by 4?

T=2π√(m/k). Multiplying both by 4 leaves the ratio, and hence the period, unchanged; increasing m alone slows the motion by a factor of 2. The dimensional analysis lesson already anticipated that the period must be √(m/k) times a constant.
Conserved Quantities Connect the Local and the Global
An undamped spring satisfies m x″=−kx. The sum of kinetic and potential energy, E=mx′²/2+kx²/2, is a conserved quantity. Here m and k are assumed to be positive constants, with no external forces.

Differentiating E gives E′=mx′x″+kxx′=x′(mx″+kx)=0. The equation of motion makes the bracket vanish, so the energy never changes. Conservation is derived from the law of motion, not posited as an extra guess.
Once the damping term c x′ (c>0) is added, what is the rate of change of the energy?
The equation is mx″+cx′+kx=0; substituting gives E′=−cx′²≤0. Mechanical energy dissipates, so the undamped conservation conclusion no longer carries over.
Potential Energy and the Energy Method

A conservative force satisfies F(x)=−V′(x) (the spring's F=−kx corresponds to V=kx²/2), and the work done depends only on the endpoints: W=−ΔV. The energy method yields qualitative conclusions without solving the equation: conservation of the total energy E=½mv²+V confines the motion to the region V≤E, with turning points given by V(x)=E.
Pull the spring to x₀ and release it: E=½kx₀²; at position x the speed satisfies ½mv²=½k(x₀²−x²) — v(x) is obtained directly, without solving the second-order equation.
What can the energy method tell you for the potential energy V(x)=x⁴/4? What if no explicit solution can be found?

E=½mv²+x⁴/4 is conserved (below we take m=1 and write ½v²+x⁴/4): the motion is confined to |x|≤(4E)^(1/4), the speed vanishes at the endpoints and reverses, and the orbit is symmetric and periodic. The period integral need not be elementary, but the qualitative conclusions (accessible region, turning points, symmetry) do not depend on an explicit solution — such is the value of qualitative analysis.
The One-Dimensional Wave Equation

Small transverse vibrations of a string lead to ∂²u/∂t²=c²∂²u/∂x², with c=√(tension/linear density); u(x,t) is a function of two variables — for partial derivatives and the chain rule in two variables, see 06, Lesson 09. The general solution is u=f(x−ct)+g(x+ct): any shape propagates in both directions at speed c, and solutions may be superposed — the mathematical definition of a "wave". This general solution is for the unforced one-dimensional equation on the whole real line with constant c>0 and sufficiently smooth profiles, twice differentiable for classical solutions. A finite string also needs boundary conditions; see lesson 07.
An initial displacement f(x) released from rest evolves into u(x,t)=½[f(x−ct)+f(x+ct)]: the initial shape splits into two halves, each propagating to one side at speed c (the d'Alembert solution).
Why does "any waveform propagates while keeping its shape" correspond exactly to this equation?

For u=f(x−ct): u_tt=c²f″ and u_xx=f″, so u_tt=c²u_xx holds automatically, and likewise for g(x+ct); the equation is linear, so the sum of the two branches is again a solution. Conversely, the general solution of this equation is exactly the sum of two traveling waves — linear structure + second derivatives = shape-preserving propagation in both directions.
Newton's Law of Cooling: The Physics of a First-Order Equation

The rate of change of an object's temperature is proportional to its difference from the surroundings: T′=−k(T−T₀). It is a direct physical instance of the separable and first-order linear equations of 11 (explicit solution T=T₀+(T(0)−T₀)e^(−kt)); heat exchange among several objects becomes a system of equations — the prototype of a thermal network.
Coffee at 85°C sits in a 25°C room, with k=0.1/minute: T=25+60e^(−0.1t). After 30 minutes T=25+60e⁻³≈28°C; the temperature difference halves every ln2/k≈6.9 minutes.
How many half-lives does it take to reduce the temperature difference to 1% of its initial value? Does it depend on the initial difference?

1%=2⁻ⁿ gives n=log₂100≈6.6 half-lives, independent of the initial value — exponential decay cares only about proportions. Conversely, using the cooling law to infer the "time of death" (given normal body temperature and the ambient temperature) is a standard application in forensics: measure k, measure the current temperature, and solve for t.
Standing Waves, Boundaries, and Discrete Frequencies

With both ends of the string fixed (u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0), the wave equation admits only sinusoidal modes whose "nodes fall exactly at the ends": uₙ(x,t)=sin(nπx/L)·cos(nπct/L). The boundary conditions sift the continuum of wavelengths into a discrete spectrum — frequencies can only be integer multiples of the fundamental frequency. This is a mathematical preview of "confinement leads to quantization": energy levels, like frequencies, are sifted out by boundary conditions.

For a string with L=1: the fundamental angular frequency πc and the second harmonic 2πc. If the initial shape is exactly f(x)=sin(πx), only the fundamental mode is excited — superposition of the traveling waves reflected at the two ends (the d'Alembert viewpoint) yields the same conclusion.
Why can a string fixed at both ends not carry a "half-wavelength standing wave" of the sin(πx/(2L)) type?

At x=L it takes the value sin(π/2)=1≠0, violating the boundary condition. "Which solutions exist" is decided by the interval and the boundary values, not by dynamical preference — turning "which frequencies are allowed" into a geometric question is a standard move of mathematical physics (the gateway to the mathematics of quantum theory).
Coulomb's Law and the Inverse Square

The force between two point charges is F=k q₁q₂/r², directed along the line joining them (like charges repel, unlike attract), structurally identical to universal gravitation. The inverse-square behavior is a geometric outcome: as the field crosses a sphere, the same amount is spread over 4πr². In the language of fields: a charge assigns an electric field E to each point, and a test charge feels the force qE; problems with multiple charges are linearized by the superposition principle — isomorphic to 04 Linear Algebra.

Electron and proton: the ratio of electrostatic force to gravity is ≈ ke²/(Gmₚmₑ)≈10³⁹ — electricity overwhelms gravity, which is why matter is neutral as a whole. Two 1-coulomb opposite charges 1 meter apart attract with F=k·1·1/1²=9×10⁹ newtons — charges of macroscopic size reveal astonishing forces.
Three equal charges sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle: outline the reasoning for the force on a test charge at the center.

Let each vertex charge be q, the central test charge Q and each vertex distance r. The three forces have magnitude k|qQ|/r² and directions separated by 120°, so their vector sum is exactly zero. The central field is also zero. Choosing one symmetry axis does not give a nonzero force direction: a 120° rotation must leave the net vector unchanged, which only the zero in-plane vector satisfies. The quantity kq/r² is a field, not the force including Q.
The Galilean Transformation and Relativity

In a reference frame translated with velocity v along the x direction, the coordinates are replaced by x′=x−vt, t′=t — written as a matrix, a shear-type linear mixing of (x,t). The Galilean principle of relativity: the laws of mechanics take the same form in all inertial frames (experiments in a cabin moving at constant velocity detect nothing of the ship's speed). But the speed of light c delivered by Maxwell's electromagnetic theory does not obey "velocities add and subtract" — the contradiction was finally resolved by special relativity: replace it with the Lorentz transformation x′=γ(x−vt), γ=1/√(1−v²/c²), and time is no longer absolute.

A ball thrown at speed u aboard the ship has speed u+v as seen from the shore; light, whatever the speed of its source, is always c — the clash between these two kinds of "velocity composition" points straight to the revolution of 1905.

Under the Galilean transformation, how do the distance between two points at one instant, the time interval, and velocity each transform? Is "simultaneity" still absolute under the Lorentz transformation?

Distance (measured simultaneously) and time interval are unchanged; velocities compose as u′=u−v. Under the Lorentz transformation "simultaneity" depends on the reference frame — absolute time is a low-speed approximation, not a logical necessity. The 2×2 matrices (see 04, Lesson 03) carry all of the kinematics here.
The Continuum: From Strings to Fluids

A string is a continuum with its matter compressed into one dimension: each position x carries a displacement u(x,t), and local tension plus Newton's laws yields the wave equation. The same recipe climbs in dimension: a fluid is described by a density ρ(x,t) and a velocity field v(x,t); conservation of mass gives ∂ρ/∂t+∇·(ρv)=0, and conservation of momentum gives the Euler/Navier–Stokes equations; sound is precisely the propagation of pressure disturbances — a close cousin of the wave equation. The shared technique is linearization: for small disturbances, discard the higher-order terms.

String: tension provides the restoring force → u_tt=c²u_xx. Gas: a compressed region pushes on its surroundings → the pressure disturbance satisfies p_tt=c²p_xx, where c is the speed of sound (about 340 m/s in air). One mathematical skeleton (a hyperbolic equation) carries strings, sound, and water waves.
Why is conservation of mass written as ∂ρ/∂t+∇·(ρv)=0? What is ∫ρv·n dA?

For a fixed region: the rate at which the interior mass decreases = the net rate of outflow; ρv is the mass flux density, the surface integral ∫ρv·n dA is the mass leaving through the boundary per unit time, the divergence theorem turns it into a volume integral, and rearranging gives the equation. Conservation law + localization = the standard generator of partial differential equations (see the 15 and 11 branch pages for the continuum route).

A Model Must State Its Assumptions

A model is a simplification that keeps the key mechanisms for a specific question. It should state its variables, units, parameters, assumptions, and scope of validity, and be checked against new data; a good fit does not mean a correct mechanism.

The population model N′=rN implicitly assumes a constant per-capita growth rate and unlimited resources. It may fit the short run, yet it predicts unbounded growth in the long run. With limited resources, consider the logistic model.
To predict a commute with 'distance = speed × time', which assumptions are needed?

The speed should be the average over the whole trip, or the speed should be assumed constant; one should also state whether waits and detours are included. Parameters should be estimated for the route and time of day in question, and the prediction error checked.
A Complete Case: Exponential or Logistic?

Modeling runs the full pipeline: question (will growth stay exponential forever?) → variables and units → candidate models (N′=rN vs. N′=rN(1−N/K)) → fitting parameters to data → testing on new data → stating the scope of validity. The logistic model writes 'limited resources' directly into the equation, with K the carrying capacity.

While N is far below K, the logistic model is nearly exponential, and both fit the early data equally well — the first half alone cannot distinguish the mechanisms. Once the data approach K, the exponential model runs systematically high and loses. r is fixed by the early growth rate, K by the leveling-off level.
Both models fit the first half of the data. What does this show, and what else does model selection rest on?

It shows the first half has poor identifiability: for N≪K the two models' predictions nearly coincide. Selection must also lean on the second half or on new data, and on whether the mechanism is plausible. The equilibrium and stability analysis of the logistic equation appears in Lesson 04 of 11. Choosing a model is choosing a mechanism — not choosing the prettier fit.
Sensitivity: What If a Parameter Is a Little Off?

Model outputs often depend on uncertain parameters. Sensitivity analysis fixes everything else, varies one parameter, and watches the output respond; it reveals which quantities deserve the most careful measurement.

The compound-interest model A=P(1+r)ⁿ (a constant rate per period): doubling P doubles A, while the effect of the interest rate compounds over n periods. Long-range extrapolation is especially sensitive to the growth-rate assumption.
With P=100 and n=2, what do r=0.1 and r=0.2 give? Can this be treated as a guaranteed return?
121 and 144, respectively. No — this is arithmetic under a constant-rate assumption; real returns, fees, and risks need separate modeling.
Nondimensionalization: Fewer Parameters, More Essence

Substituting variables built from the problem's intrinsic scales compresses the equation's parameters into a few dimensionless numbers. Three benefits: fewer parameters, experiments that can be scaled, and a clear view of which terms dominate. Dimensional analysis is the entry point (see Lesson 01 of 15); here we treat the equation itself.

Logistic N′=rN(1−N/K): set u=N/K and τ=rt, and the equation becomes u′=u(1−u). Of the three parameters (r, K, N₀) only the combination u₀=N₀/K remains — all logistic growth is one and the same curve, stretched and squeezed.
How many parameters remain after nondimensionalizing m·dv/dt=−mg, v(0)=v₀?

Take the velocity scale v₀ (requiring v₀≠0; for release from rest the scale must instead come from, e.g., the drop height) and the time scale v₀/g, and set u=v/v₀: the equation becomes du/dτ=−1 with u(0)=1. The mass m disappears entirely — the reason heavy objects fall at the same speed is revealed automatically.
Fitting, Extrapolation, and Overfitting

Prediction inside the observed input range is interpolation in the broad predictive sense, while strict mathematical interpolation also requires passing through specified data points; regression allows residuals. Prediction outside the range is extrapolation and relies more heavily on mechanism assumptions. Overfitting means good training fit but poor generalization. Many parameters increase the risk, but parameters need not outnumber observations. Holdout validation, regularization and comparison with simpler models help diagnose it.

Two points with distinct x-coordinates determine one line but admit infinitely many quadratic or higher-degree polynomials through them. At n distinct nodes, exactly one polynomial of degree at most n−1 interpolates the values. This is a full-rank linear problem, not a theorem that arbitrary models with as many parameters as data points fit perfectly or uniquely. Zero training error alone proves neither a mechanism nor generalization.
What is the relation between 'the first half of the data cannot distinguish exponential from logistic' and overfitting?

Both can reflect insufficient information, but identifiability and overfitting differ. When N≪K, exponential and logistic predictions are close: this is a practical identifiability difficulty in the observed range, not necessarily strict structural nonidentifiability. Overfitting concerns poor generalization and can occur with fewer parameters than observations. Broader observations, independent validation and simpler comparisons help; training error alone is insufficient.
Spreading on Networks

A network SIR model has susceptible, infected and removed nodes, with infection along edges and recovery at rate γ. Structure affects spread, but an infected hub does not necessarily infect every leaf. The friendship paradox is an aggregate sampling effect: choose an edge uniformly in a finite undirected network with at least one edge, then choose an endpoint. Nodes are sampled in proportion to degree, giving mean degree Σdᵢ²/Σdᵢ≥Σdᵢ/N by nonnegative degree variance. It does not say every person's friends have more friends. Choosing a person first and then a neighbor gives a different distribution that must be analyzed separately.

The hub of a star has many transmission routes, but whether each transmission succeeds depends on infection and recovery rates and elapsed time. One round need not infect every leaf. A chain has fewer routes; speed and final outbreak size also depend on the dynamics. Structure describes opportunities, not a replacement for a probability model.

Why is 'immunizing the friends of a randomly chosen person' usually more effective than 'immunizing a randomly chosen person'? Explain with the friendship paradox and the handshaking lemma (Lesson 03 of 08).

The friendship paradox says a randomly chosen friend has a higher average degree; cutting off high-degree nodes first pushes the effective transmission rate below the threshold faster. On networks the epidemic threshold depends on the first and second moments of the degree distribution — graph theory (08), probability (09), and dynamical systems (11) converge here.
Feedback Loops: Positive, Negative, and Systems

Feedback sends output back to influence input. Negative feedback acts against a deviation; positive feedback reinforces it. Multiplying the signs around a loop identifies its feedback sign, not its stability. Excessive gain, delay or a discrete step can make negative feedback oscillate or diverge. Stability requires the actual equations: xₙ₊₁=−2xₙ reverses a deviation but doubles its magnitude each step.

Thermostat: temperature below the set point → heating on → temperature recovers → heating off (a negative loop, oscillating mildly around the set point). Bank run: a rumor → a few withdrawals → the queue lengthens → more panic (a positive loop, until collapse). Newton's law of cooling in 11 is the continuous version of negative feedback: the larger the temperature difference, the faster the heat loss.
Is market-price adjustment of supply and demand positive or negative feedback? Draw the loop and label the direction of deviation at each step.

Price above equilibrium can increase supply and reduce demand, creating a surplus that pushes price down: this is negative feedback by sign. Convergence depends on adjustment speed, supply and demand responses and delays; overcorrection can oscillate or diverge. Draw the signed loop, then analyze an explicit model's equilibria and stability. Counting negative signs alone is insufficient.

Extending Number Systems Repairs the Boundaries of the Operations

The natural numbers serve counting, but 3−5 is not among them; the integers accommodate subtraction and the rationals accommodate division by nonzero divisors; the reals complete the structure needed for limits; the complex numbers allow squares equal to −1.
x²=2 has no solution in the rationals but ±√2 in the reals. x²+1=0 has no solution in the reals but ±i in the complex numbers. Saying 'no solution' requires naming the number system.
What happens to x+3=1 in the natural numbers versus the integers?
No solution in the natural numbers; in the integers the solution is −2. The rules of the operations and the set of solutions depend on the universe under discussion.
Axioms, Definitions, and Theorems Have Different Jobs

Definitions fix what terms mean, axioms lay down a system's basic assumptions, and theorems follow from them logically. The validity of a proof depends on its premises; a picture or an authority is not a proof.

In the Euclidean plane, the angles of a triangle sum to 180°; on a sphere, a geodesic triangle can exceed 180°. For instance, the North Pole together with two equatorial points 90° apart forms a spherical triangle with three right angles.
Does the spherical example refute Euclidean geometry?
No. It changes what the space and 'straight lines' mean — the premises differ. When comparing mathematical statements, compare their definitions and assumptions at the same time.
Infinitesimals and the Birth of Limits

The 'infinitesimals' of Newton and Leibniz worked but were logically murky: divide by an increment first, then let the increment vanish — self-contradictory in sequence (Berkeley mocked them as 'the ghosts of departed quantities'). In the nineteenth century Cauchy began, and Weierstrass completed, the reconstruction of limits with ε-δ, translating 'approaches arbitrarily closely' into a finite language of inequalities (the formal definition appears in Lesson 01 of 06).

To find the fluxion of x², one first computes (x+o)²−x², divides by o to get 2x+o, and then 'lets o be zero' to obtain 2x — the increment is first treated as nonzero and then as zero, precisely the point under attack. The ε-δ definition never lets the increment 'become zero'; it only requires |f(x)−L|<ε whenever 0<|x−a|<δ — note the punctured condition excluding x=a, exactly where the difference quotient has no definition.
Does the ε-δ definition answer 'what is an infinitesimal', or does it bypass the question?

It bypasses rather than answers: it stops talking about infinitely small quantities and expresses 'as close as desired' using only the finite positive numbers ε and δ. This is a successful translation — restating an intractable infinite object as a checkable finite statement; mathematics often substitutes reformulation for frontal assault.
The Discovery of Non-Euclidean Geometry

Euclid's parallel postulate was held for two millennia to be a self-evident truth, yet it was the axiom most resembling a theorem, and every attempted 'proof' smuggled in an equivalent assumption. Replacing it (no parallels through an external point, or more than one) yields sphere-like and hyperbolic geometries, each with its own models and internally consistent. Conclusion: axioms are chosen starting points, and truth is relative to the system.

On a sphere, take 'straight lines' to be great circles: any two great circles intersect, so no parallel passes through an external point, and geodesic triangles have angle sums above 180° — the spherical triangle of the previous lesson is this model's intuitive cousin (a strict model must identify antipodal points, giving elliptic geometry: two great circles on the sphere meet in two points, conflicting with the Euclidean 'two lines meet in at most one point').
After non-Euclidean geometries were accepted, what became of the belief that 'Euclidean geometry is the truth about physical space'?

It was demoted from the sole necessity to one optional model: general relativity describes gravity with curved geometry, and which geometry fits physical space became an empirical question settled by measurement. Mathematics supplies consistent systems; which one applies is left to physics — the division of labor between the axiomatic method and empirical science was drawn here.
Philosophy of Mathematics: Three Schools and Incompleteness

Logicism (Frege, Russell) sought to reduce mathematics to logic; formalism (Hilbert) emphasized formal systems and consistency proofs; intuitionism (Brouwer) emphasized constructions and restricted unrestricted excluded middle. Incompleteness has essential hypotheses: a consistent, effectively axiomatized system expressing enough basic arithmetic cannot decide every sentence in its language. The second theorem, with the usual provability-coding conditions, limits proving its own consistency internally. Not every consistent system is incomplete, nor is a sentence unprovable in every stronger system.

Gödel encoded 'statements about proofs' as natural numbers (Gödel numbering) and then used the diagonal to construct 'this proposition is unprovable' — the same method as Cantor's diagonal (Lesson 07 of 01) and the halting problem (Lesson 04 of 14).
How does 'axioms are chosen starting points' (Lesson 02) connect with the disagreements among the three schools? What does incompleteness show?

The schools differ over mathematical objects and acceptable proofs; arbitrary consistent axioms alone do not capture those differences. Gödel's conclusion applies to effectively axiomatized theories strong enough for arithmetic: under those conditions, consistency and sentence-completeness cannot coexist. Without effective axiomatizability, true arithmetic is a consistent complete theory, but its axioms cannot be effectively enumerated. The theorem limits particular formal methods rather than mathematical proof itself.
Reading Theorems, Writing Proofs: Mathematical Communication

Reading a theorem in four steps: ① what are the hypotheses and the conclusion; ② where does the proof use each hypothesis; ③ drop a hypothesis and hunt for a counterexample; ④ produce an example of your own. Writing a proof runs in reverse: state the strategy first (contradiction/induction/construction), then give each step its reason, and close by returning to the conclusion. Educational research agrees: retelling to others and spaced redoing beat rereading by far — the 'closed-book recall' of this course was designed for exactly that.

For a continuous real function on a nonempty closed bounded interval, isolate the hypotheses. Without continuity, set f(0)=0 and f(x)=1/x for x>0 on [0,1]; it is unbounded. Without closedness, f(x)=x on (0,1) never attains its supremum 1. Without boundedness, f(x)=x on [0,∞) has no maximum. Removing one key hypothesis at a time identifies its role.
Rewrite 'the first n positive odd numbers sum to n²' from the induction lesson of 01 in the communication format 'strategy first, then steps'.

Strategy: induction — the base case lays the foundation and the step passes it along. Steps: ① n=1: 1=1²; ② assume the first k terms sum to k²; ③ add the (k+1)-st odd number 2k+1 to get (k+1)²; ④ this holds for all n, each step using only definitions and the induction hypothesis. Stating 'which hypothesis was used where' lets the reader check — checkability is what separates mathematical communication from persuasion.
